strengths: First systematic study of instruction fine-tuning for generative retrieval (GR), a genuinely under-explored direction, with a clear framing of docid design, corpus indexing, and docid decoding as the three levers for zero-shot adaptation.
Releases ZeroGR-Train, a large (41M pairs, 69 tasks, 6 domains) instruction-annotated IR training corpus, which is a useful community resource.

Comprehensive ablation suite: docid design comparison (Fig. 5), scaling of instruction-tuning task diversity (Fig. 4), number of pseudo-queries, model size, and decoding strategy (Fig. 6), which strengthens the empirical story beyond a single headline number.
The reverse-annealed decoding strategy is a simple, sensible mechanism for trading off precision and recall in docid decoding, and the decoding ablation supports the design motivation.
Evaluation spans two heterogeneous benchmarks (MAIR, BEIR) with both seen and unseen task splits, and per-task results are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Headline claims are stronger than the evidence. On BEIR (Table 4), ZeroGR-3B (48.1) clearly underperforms E5-mistral-7B (55.7), OpenAI Embed (54.2), BGE-Large (51.8), and others; on the MAIR unseen subset (Table 3) it averages 26.7 vs. 41.9 for E5-mistral-7B. 'Zero-shot generalization' — the paper's central claim — is precisely where the model is weakest, so claims of SOTA/establishing a new state of the art need substantial qualification.

Comparison cost asymmetry is unaddressed: ZeroGR requires training a task-specific generative index per corpus/task (docid generation, pseudo-query generation, retriever fine-tuning), whereas dense baselines require only query/document encoding. No indexing-time cost, latency, or scalability analysis is provided, despite scalability being a known bottleneck for GR (the paper cites Pradeep et al., 2023 on this) and 'scalable' appearing in the title.

Potential train/test contamination is not carefully controlled: ZeroGR-Train is drawn from MAIR training splits, and BEIR-Train splits (e.g., NFCorpus, Quora, SciDocs-related data) are explicitly included in the instruction-tuning mixture, while evaluation uses BEIR and MAIR test sets. The seen/unseen split exists for MAIR, but the BEIR protocol is not analyzed from this perspective, and comparisons to dense baselines trained without this data may be conflated.

The docid generator relies on GPT-4o outputs for supervision, introducing dependence on a proprietary model, and the docid conflict/ambiguity behavior of the generated docids on large corpora is not quantified (only conflict-rate distributions on small dev tasks).

Inconsistencies and sloppiness reduce confidence: text says 'all 12 tasks from BEIR' but tables report 11; the code/data footnote (p.2) is empty; Table 3 avg. numbers are hard to reconcile with the domain averages in Table 2; duplicated rows appear in Table 5; typo '..both cases..' in the introduction.

Key design choices lack ablation depth: hyperparameters of reverse annealing (k, m, Tmax) are not studied; B (queries per document) interacts with indexing cost and its cost-benefit is only shown up to 16; no comparison against recent competitive GR systems beyond TIGER/GENRE/GENRET/GLEN on a subset of BEIR datasets.

Significance is somewhat incremental: each component (LLM-generated docids/summaries, pseudo-query generation, temperature scheduling) exists in prior work; the novelty is mainly in assembling them under instruction tuning, and the strongest results are competitive rather than clearly superior to dense retrieval.

strengths: Timely problem: extending generative retrieval (GR) to zero-shot/instruction-driven settings is an interesting and relatively unexplored direction, and the paper claims to be the first to apply instruction fine-tuning to GR.
Release of ZeroGR-Train (41M query-document pairs across 69 tasks and 6 domains) is potentially a useful community resource.

Systematic ablation structure: the paper examines docid designs, number of pseudo-queries, model size, instruction-tuning task diversity, and decoding strategies, providing some useful empirical insights (e.g., pseudo-query count vs. accuracy, docid conflict rates).
Reverse-annealed decoding is a reasonable, simple idea for trading off precision and recall in docid generation, with a sensible motivation.
weaknesses: The central claim is not well supported and is partially contradicted by the paper's own results. The paper claims SOTA and superiority over strong dense baselines, yet on the MAIR average (Table 2) ZeroGR-3B (41.1) clearly loses to E5-mistral-7B (46.8) and GritLM-7B (47.0), and on BEIR (Table 4) its average (48.1) is below BGE-Large (51.8) and far below E5-mistral-7B (55.7). The headline comparison to OpenAI Embed-v3 is marginal (+0.5) and appears cherry-picked.

The zero-shot generalization claim is undermined by Table 3: on the unseen MAIR subset, ZeroGR-3B averages 26.7, the lowest among all compared models (BM25: 32.8, E5-mistral-7B: 41.9, OpenAI: 32.8). This directly contradicts the framing that ZeroGR generalizes better to unseen tasks.

The 'zero-shot' setting is questionable at deployment: the generative retriever must be trained for each evaluated task/corpus on generated pseudo-queries (Section 5.4). Requiring per-corpus LM training is a substantial indexing cost, and the paper provides no analysis of indexing time/compute or corpus-size scalability, despite claiming a 'scalable framework'. GR's known weakness at large corpus scale is not addressed.

Potential train/test contamination: training data is drawn from MAIR training splits (the same benchmark suite used for evaluation), and the seen/unseen split is self-defined by the authors. The BEIR-train and MTEB data usage in scaling experiments further blurs the zero-shot boundary. No decontamination analysis is provided.

The reverse annealing contribution is thin: per Figure 6, greedy decoding matches it on Acc@1 (45.7 vs 45.7) and beam search nearly matches on all metrics (42.1 Acc@1, 52.6 nDCG, similar Recall@100), so the reported advantage is small and the scheduling hyperparameters (k, m, Tmax) are not analyzed.

Reproducibility and consistency problems: the code/data footnote is empty ('available at' with no URL); Section 6.3 says '60 tasks' while Table 1 and the conclusion say 69; the conclusion says 'seven BEIR datasets' while the text says 11-12; Table 5 contains duplicated rows (ProofWiki, Stacks, Competition-Math); several typos (e.g., double periods, 'prior studies has shown').

Missing standard experimental rigor: no statistical significance testing, no variance over seeds, no efficiency/inference-cost comparison against the dense baselines that vastly outperform it, and several GR baselines in Table 4 have missing entries, weakening the GR-to-GR comparison.

Novelty is moderate: the components largely recombine existing techniques (pseudo-query generation a la DSI-QG, text/summary docids, constrained decoding with temperature schedules) with instruction tuning; the framing as a new paradigm is stronger than the technical novelty.

strengths: Novel and meaningful research direction: this appears to be the first systematic attempt at instruction fine-tuning for generative retrieval, extending GR to zero-shot/heterogeneous settings that prior GR work has largely ignored.
Release of ZeroGR-Train, a large (41M pairs, 69 tasks, 6 domains) and diverse open instruction-tuning corpus for IR, which is a useful community resource.

Comprehensive experimental design: evaluation on both MAIR and BEIR with baselines spanning sparse, single-task dense, multi-task dense, and instruction-tuned dense retrieval, plus systematic ablations on task-diversity scaling, docid design, pseudo-query count, model size, and decoding strategy.
The reverse-annealed decoding analysis (Fig. 6) is a nice, well-motivated study showing a concrete precision/recall trade-off vs. greedy, nucleus, and beam decoding.
The docid design comparison (Fig. 5 left) against Random/Sentence/Paragraph/Query/Summary/RQ-VAE under controlled conditions is a valuable empirical contribution to the GR literature.
weaknesses: The headline claim of outperforming strong dense baselines is not supported by the main results: on MAIR (Table 2), ZeroGR-3B averages 41.1 Acc@1 vs. 46.8 for E5-mistral-7B and 47.0 for GritLM-7B; on BEIR it averages 48.1 vs. 55.7 for E5-mistral-7B and 54.2 for OpenAI Embedding. The 'new SOTA' claim holds only within the GR category, and the abstract/intro overstate the evidence.

More seriously, on the MAIR unseen subset (Table 3), ZeroGR-3B averages 26.7, which is below BM25 (32.8) and far below E5-mistral-7B (41.9) and Contriever (40.4). This directly undercuts the central zero-shot generalization claim, yet the text describes it as 'competitive.'

The 'zero-shot' framing is questionable. The model is instruction-tuned on 41M pairs extracted from MAIR training splits, and then evaluated on the MAIR 'seen' subset; the retriever is also trained separately per evaluated task, requiring per-corpus index construction. This is few-shot/instruction-tuned rather than zero-shot, and the MAIR-derived training data raises benchmark contamination concerns.

Notable internal inconsistencies: the number of training tasks is stated as 69 in Section 5.1 but 60 in Figure 4; BEIR is described as 'all 12 tasks' in Section 5.2 but Table 2/4 report 11 tasks; the conclusion says 'seven BEIR datasets' while Table 4 lists twelve; the code/data footnote (footnote 1) is empty ('available at' with no URL), harming reproducibility.

No efficiency analysis: GR requires per-corpus retriever training and constrained tree decoding, but there is no reporting of indexing time, latency, or memory versus a single forward-pass dense retriever, which is essential for assessing practical significance.

Several strong baselines and controls are missing: no comparison with recent competitive GR systems trained at comparable scale, no variance/significance testing, and docid generation depends on GPT-4o without ablation of that dependency or its cost.

Some baseline numbers appear anomalous (e.g., GritLM-7B BEIR average of 45.0, well below its typical reported performance), and metrics like nDCG@10 and Acc@1 are mixed across benchmarks without per-task alignment, making cross-paradigm comparisons harder to interpret.

strengths: Novel and timely direction: first systematic investigation of instruction fine-tuning for generative retrieval, extending GR to zero-shot settings via natural language task instructions; this is a genuine gap in the GR literature and well-motivated.

OpenInstIR is a substantial resource contribution: 69 IR tasks across 6 domains with 41M query-document pairs, claimed to be the largest open-source instructed retrieval training set, with careful train/eval type separation (Table 5) to validate zero-shot generalization.

Comprehensive and well-designed ablation studies: task diversity scaling (Fig. 2), docid design comparisons against strong alternatives including RQ-VAE (Fig. 3, Table 7), decoding strategy comparison (Fig. 5), query count and model size scaling — all with controlled apples-to-apples setups.

Establishes new state-of-the-art among generative retrieval methods on BEIR (48.1 vs. 31.0–41.1 for prior GR), with a fair GR baseline (TIGER retrained on the same OpenInstIR data), plus a useful ablation (Table 13) isolating the query generator's contribution (+6.4 avg).
Good reproducibility: code release, detailed implementation details, prompts, hyperparameters, baseline links, algorithm pseudocode, and efficiency cost analysis (Table 10).
weaknesses: The central claim of strong zero-shot generalization is weaker than presented: on the unseen MAIR subset (Table 8), ZeroGR-3B averages 26.7, well below Contriever (40.4), E5-Base (40.4), E5-Mistral-7B (41.9), and even BM25 (32.8). The abstract's framing ('competitive performance... new state-of-the-art') leans heavily on beating prior GR methods rather than demonstrating parity with the dense systems that define the practical bar.

Overall performance still lags strong dense retrievers: on MAIR, ZeroGR-3B (41.1) trails E5-Mistral-7B (46.8) and GritLM-7B (47.0) by ~6 points; on BEIR (Table 9) it trails E5-Mistral-7B and OpenAI Embed by ~6-8 points. The paper is honest about this (Appendix C) but the contribution is then primarily 'best GR so far' rather than a competitive retrieval system.

A significant practical limitation: the generative retriever M must be retrained from a Llama-3B-Instruct base for every new corpus/task (indexing = model training), incurring high one-time indexing cost (~1.8h for 100K docs vs ~8 min for dense), and evaluation is restricted to corpora under 1M documents. Scalability of the core recipe to realistic corpora remains unaddressed.

Some technical novelty is incremental: the docid generator is essentially an LLM-based title/keyword docid (building on title and summary docid prior work), pseudo-query generation follows DSI-QG with instruction conditioning, and reverse annealing is a temperature-scheduled sampling variant. Each component is reasonable but none is deeply novel; the strongest contribution is the empirical/dataset study.

Ablations rely on small dev subsets (Table 6: often <15 tasks, 37-100 queries per task), and no statistical significance or variance over seeds is reported for any comparison; several benchmark-level gaps (e.g., Fig. 5 decoding differences of <1 nDCG) may not be robust.

Minor inconsistencies: text in 7.2 says ZeroGR 'outperforms... GritLM-7B' on BEIR while Table 9 shows GritLM at 45.0 vs 48.1 for ZeroGR but GritLM outperforms ZeroGR on several datasets; Table 12 lists TIGER with reverse-annealing decoding although it is presented as a baseline; BEIR evaluation uses 11-12 of 18 standard datasets.

strengths: First systematic investigation of instruction fine-tuning for generative retrieval, a relatively unexplored direction; the paper clearly positions itself against prior instruction-tuned dense retrievers.

Releases OpenInstIR, a large (41M pairs, 69 tasks, 6 domains) open-source instructed retrieval training dataset with documented construction methodology (Table 4), enabling future work on zero-shot GR.

Unusually thorough ablation coverage for a GR paper: docid design (6 alternatives), docid distribution/conflict analysis, decoding strategies, number of pseudo-queries, task diversity scaling, and model-size scaling, each with a clear motivating analysis (e.g., Figure 4 trie analysis, Table 13 query-generator swap on TIGER).

Honest reporting in several places: the paper acknowledges underperformance vs. strong dense retrievers on BEIR, admits limitations on corpus scale (>1M docs) and model size (3B), and provides an efficiency analysis (Table 10).
Implementation details (learning rates, epochs, model choices, prompts in Appendix E) and promised code release support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Headline claims are stronger than the evidence. On MAIR, ZeroGR-3B (41.1) is clearly below E5-Mistral-7B (46.8) and GritLM-7B (47.0), and on the unseen MAIR subset it averages 26.7 — worse than most strong dense baselines (E5-Mistral 41.9, Contriever 40.4). 'State-of-the-art among GR methods' rests on comparison with essentially one recent GR baseline (TIGER), and 'on par with OpenAI Embed-v3' refers only to the Small variant.

The comparison with TIGER in Table 3/12 is confounded: TIGER is re-implemented with the authors' reverse-annealing decoding and query generator, so it is unclear whether ZeroGR's docid design or the shared components drive the gains; a cleaner docid-only comparison is only partially provided (Table 13).

The proposed reverse-annealing decoding shows marginal and inconsistent gains: in Figure 5 it ties greedy decoding on Acc@1 (45.7) and is essentially tied with beam search on nDCG@10 (52.5 vs 52.6), only clearly winning on Recall@100; the added complexity relative to standard sampling is hard to justify.

The reverse-annealing and docid-generator components are conceptually simple (temperature schedule over tree-constrained sampling; GPT-4o-distilled keyword titles as docids); the paper's contribution is largely empirical/engineering rather than methodological, and the core insight reduces to instruction-tuned doc2query.

Potential train/test contamination: OpenInstIR is built from training splits of public datasets including BEIR-related sources, and the query generator is trained on tasks overlapping evaluation domains (Figure 2 shows BEIR-Train and MTEB-Train stages); the seen/unseen MAIR split mitigates but does not eliminate leakage concerns for the BEIR results.

Scalability of the paradigm is fundamentally questionable and only partially addressed: GR requires per-corpus model training (hours per 100K documents vs minutes for dense indexing, Table 10), and evaluation is restricted to corpora under 1M documents — a serious practical limitation for the claimed 'generalizable and scalable framework'.

Internal inconsistencies suggest rushed preparation: the abstract and Section 5.1 state 69 tasks while Appendix A states 66, and the Figure 2 caption says OpenInstIR includes 60 tasks; Table 8's 'seen' subset caption is misplaced relative to the data layout.

Statistical rigor is thin: results are single-run averages over small query samples (Table 6 uses 37–100 queries per task), with no significance testing or variance estimates, making small reported differences difficult to interpret.

ZeroGR underperforms even BM25 on several unseen MAIR tasks (e.g., Table 8 unseen subset average 26.7 vs BM25 32.8), which undercuts the central zero-shot generalization narrative on the harder, more diverse split.

strengths: First systematic study of instruction fine-tuning for generative retrieval (GR), addressing a genuine and under-explored limitation of the paradigm (poor zero-shot generalization of GR models).
Contribution of OpenInstIR, a large-scale (41M pairs, 69 tasks, 6 domains) open-source instructed retrieval training corpus, which enables the study and should benefit follow-up work.

Comprehensive and well-designed ablations: task diversity scaling (Fig. 2), six docid design alternatives including a fair RQ-VAE comparison (Fig. 3, Table 7), docid conflict/distribution analysis (Fig. 4), decoding strategy comparison (Fig. 5), and model-size/query-count scaling. The cross-component ablation (Table 13) isolating the query generator's contribution is particularly convincing.

Fair baseline practices: TIGER is retrained on OpenInstIR for an apples-to-apples GR comparison, and a broad set of sparse, single-task, multi-task, and instruction-tuned dense retrievers is included.
Clear analysis of failure modes (Appendix C) honestly acknowledging the remaining gap to dense retrieval rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: The 'zero-shot' framing is somewhat misleading: each new corpus still requires a full retriever fine-tuning pass as the indexing step (Sec. 3, Table 10 shows ~1.8h offline indexing on a 100K-doc corpus). This is per-corpus training cost that dense retrieval does not incur, and the paper should more prominently position ZeroGR as 'training-free of supervised IR data' rather than fully zero-shot.

Absolute performance remains below strong instruction-tuned dense retrievers (41.1 vs. 46.8/47.0 for E5-Mistral-7B/GritLM-7B on MAIR; 48.1 vs. 54.2-55.7 on BEIR), and the 'state-of-the-art' claim holds only within the niche GR paradigm. The practical significance of the gap is not fully resolved.

The three components are incremental combinations of known techniques: title/summary-style semantic docids (GenRE, Li et al. 2024), doc2query-style pseudo-query indexing (DSI-QG), and temperature scheduling. Reverse-annealed decoding is a simple heuristic; notably greedy decoding matches its Acc@1 exactly (45.7), with the method only improving Recall@100.

Evaluation is limited to moderately sized corpora (<1M documents), explicitly acknowledged; scalability—a central weakness of GR—is therefore untested, weakening the 'generalizable and scalable' claim in the title.

Inconsistencies and weak spots in results presentation: OpenInstIR task count is reported as 69 (Table 1), 66 (Appendix A), and 60 (Fig. 2); the docid-generator is distilled from GPT-4o outputs, an undisclosed cost/dependency; Table 13 shows severe regressions on some tasks (e.g., NFCorpus -34.5) that are not analyzed.

The docid design relies on a fixed 6-8 word title-like sentence; the abstract-code claims (e.g., supporting tables and code) are not substantiated by any dedicated heterogeneous-format evaluation beyond noting docid conflict rates.
